strengths: The paper gives a coherent information-geometric treatment of classifier Fisher matrices, connecting the high-dimensional tensor to the pullback of a low-dimensional categorical-simplex metric.
The deterministic spectral, Löwner-order, trace, and approximation-error bounds are mathematically interesting, with detailed proofs supplied in the appendix.
The proposed randomized Gram estimator is unbiased and practically attractive for diagonal estimation: a probe requires only one reverse-mode gradient, and the diagonal variance bound is clear.
The manuscript is generally well organized and distinguishes the true Fisher, empirical Fisher, Monte Carlo estimates, and proposed randomized estimates.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is far below top-tier standards. It consists primarily of qualitative density plots from two DistilBERT settings, with no quantitative estimation error, confidence intervals, convergence-versus-probe curves, runtime or memory comparisons, scaling studies, or downstream applications.

The figures do not compare against an exact Fisher matrix or strong stochastic-estimation baselines, so they mainly illustrate inequalities that already hold in expectation rather than validating accuracy or practical usefulness.

The claimed quality guarantee applies only to diagonal entries. For off-diagonal entries, variance need not be controlled relative to the true entry; a zero off-diagonal can have positive estimator variance. Thus statements suggesting a guaranteed-quality full-tensor estimator are substantially stronger than the presented theory.

Each sample of the proposed full-matrix estimator is rank one. For a high-rank Fisher matrix, one or a few samples can be poor in spectral or Frobenius norm, yet no matrix-level concentration or approximation-error result is provided.

The comparison with Monte Carlo estimation is not fully fair: its unbounded-CV example introduces randomness from sampling a heavy-tailed input distribution, while the proposed guarantee conditions on and exhaustively sums over a fixed dataset. This does not establish superiority under matched data access and computational budgets.

The main randomized construction is a fairly direct application of a standard random sketch to a Gram-matrix factorization. The paper does not position its novelty convincingly against randomized covariance/Gram estimation, per-example-gradient sketching, or existing Fisher-estimation techniques.

Reproducibility is limited: no implementation is provided, and important experimental details such as preprocessing, probe variability, random seeds, bandwidth selection, and complete timing methodology are missing. The paper itself acknowledges that more thorough experiments and applications are left for future work.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent factor-sketch estimator of the Fisher information matrix: a random contraction followed by one reverse-mode differentiation gives an unbiased rank-one estimate, and the diagonal variance formulas are useful and mostly transparent.
The pullback perspective cleanly connects the categorical-simplex Fisher matrix to the neural-network parameter-space Fisher matrix.
The deterministic analysis supplies several explicit spectral and Loewner-order bounds, with substantial proof material included in the appendix.
The proposed estimator is architecture-agnostic and potentially inexpensive when class logits for all examples are already available.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is far below the standard expected at a top-tier AI conference. It consists primarily of density visualizations for DistilBERT on two datasets, using only 128 examples. There are no quantitative estimation-error results, repeated-trial uncertainty, runtime or memory measurements, scaling studies, or downstream applications.

The experiments never compare the estimates against an exact or sufficiently accurate reference Fisher matrix. Consequently, they do not verify unbiasedness numerically, measure variance, or show that the proposed method is more accurate or efficient than Monte Carlo, empirical-Fisher, per-example-gradient, or established structured-curvature alternatives.

The main quality claim is overstated. The bounded coefficient of variation is established only entrywise for diagonal elements; the paper gives no corresponding matrix-norm, spectral, off-diagonal, or full-tensor accuracy guarantee. A single estimate is rank one and has worst-case relative standard deviation up to sqrt(2), which is weak for practical estimation of a large matrix.

The comparison with Monte Carlo is not well controlled. Its counterexample includes random subsampling of heavy-tailed inputs, whereas the proposed estimator sums over the full fixed input dataset. This changes both the computation and the source of randomness, so it does not establish an advantage under matched data access or computational budgets.

Novelty is insufficiently established. The construction is essentially a randomized sketch of a Fisher/Gauss-Newton factor followed by an outer product, but the paper does not thoroughly compare it to prior randomized Gram-matrix estimators, Fisher-factor sampling, automatic-differentiation methods for diagonal curvature, or modern per-example-gradient tooling.

The deterministic bounds are often loose or potentially costly, and their practical value is not demonstrated. The paper itself reports that the upper bound is very loose on SST-2, while the lower-bound construction requires per-example leading-eigenvector computations.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is provided, and important details such as data selection, random seeds, KDE bandwidth, preprocessing, batching, and complete timing methodology are missing. The plots are also difficult to interpret because scales vary substantially and uncertainty is absent.

The paper explicitly leaves thorough experiments and any practical methodology or optimizer to future work. Thus, while the theoretical observations are potentially useful, the current evidence does not support the claimed practical significance or competitiveness for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, architecture-agnostic construction of an unbiased Fisher information estimator requiring only one additional backward pass.
The decomposition through the low-dimensional categorical core is insightful and yields deterministic Loewner-order bounds, spectral bounds, and approximation-error results.
The diagonal variance analysis is concrete: exact Gaussian and Rademacher formulas imply a bounded coefficient of variation, providing a useful guarantee beyond unbiasedness alone.
The main theoretical statements are accompanied by detailed proofs, and the presentation generally connects information geometry, automatic differentiation, and randomized estimation coherently.
The DistilBERT experiments on AG News and SST-2 demonstrate feasibility on a realistic modern network and qualitatively illustrate the proposed upper, unbiased, and lower estimators.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is substantially too limited for the practical claims. It contains only density visualizations on one architecture, with no ground-truth error measurements, variance-versus-sample-count study, runtime or memory benchmarks, repeated trials, strong estimator baselines, or downstream optimization application.

The advertised support for block-diagonal and full-matrix estimation is stronger than the theory provided. The bounded-relative-variance guarantee is established only for diagonal entries; off-diagonal relative error can be unbounded when the true entry is small, and a one-sample full estimator is rank one.

The comparison with Monte Carlo estimation is not fully convincing: the heavy-tailed example randomizes inputs under a population distribution, whereas the primary Fisher definition uses a fixed dataset and the proposed estimator randomizes the corresponding finite sum. A matched computational and statistical comparison is needed.

The estimator is a randomized sketch of a Gram matrix, making its novelty relative to existing randomized generalized-Gauss-Newton/Fisher and per-example-gradient methods insufficiently established. The related-work discussion does not isolate precisely what is new beyond applying random probes before backpropagation.

Several deterministic results are mathematically useful but rely on quantities such as per-example Jacobian singular values or leading core eigenvectors; the paper does not demonstrate that these bounds are sufficiently tight or economical to matter in realistic multiclass settings.

Reproducibility is limited: there is no code or pseudocode implementation, and important experimental details such as random seeds, preprocessing, probe variability, KDE settings, and timing methodology are absent.

Some exposition overstates the geometry and evidence—for example calling the Fisher tensor unique without qualification and claiming generally guaranteed estimator quality while proving the strongest guarantee only for its diagonal. Overall, the theory is promising, but the missing quantitative validation and incomplete support for broad practical claims place the work slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent progression from the Fisher geometry of categorical distributions to deterministic bounds and randomized estimators for neural-network Fisher matrices.

The central randomized construction is simple and computationally attractive: a random linear combination of score vectors can be differentiated in one backward pass, and its outer product is an unbiased estimator conditional on a fixed dataset.
The diagonal variance calculation is clear and provides a useful coefficient-of-variation bound. The experiments cover six model–dataset combinations spanning language, vision, and audio.
Most formal statements are accompanied by proofs, and the presentation is generally readable with consistent notation.
weaknesses: The main estimator is essentially a standard random sketch of a Gram matrix: if F=AA^T, draw a zero-mean probe ξ with E[ξξ^T]=I and use (Aξ)(Aξ)^T. The paper does not convincingly establish sufficient novelty beyond applying this elementary construction to score vectors, and calling it a Hutchinson FIM estimator somewhat obscures this distinction.

Claims about estimating the full metric tensor are substantially stronger than the evidence. A single estimate is rank one, the variance guarantee covers only individual diagonal entries, and all quantitative experiments evaluate only the diagonal after aggregation across 128 minibatches. There are no spectral- or Frobenius-error results, matrix-vector product tests, or downstream natural-gradient experiments.

The comparison with Monte Carlo estimation is not fully aligned. The heavy-tail argument treats inputs as population samples, whereas the proposed variance guarantee is conditional on a fixed dataset. If inputs or minibatches are sampled, the proposed estimator also inherits data-sampling variance and can depend on fourth moments. The experimental exclusion of MC on computational grounds is asserted without comparisons to vectorized per-sample-gradient or sampled-label implementations.

The empirical study is too limited for the central claims: it reports one aggregate RelMAE table, with no repetitions, uncertainty estimates, probe-count curves, per-layer error analysis, or sensitivity to batch size. The relative-error metric is also highly sensitive to near-zero Fisher entries and the fixed epsilon, while the reported speed factors omit detailed memory and wall-clock methodology.

The deterministic-bound contribution is not adequately validated. The paper does not measure bound gaps or computational costs on the studied networks, and several bounds depend on Jacobian singular values that may themselves be impractical to obtain.

The description of λ_C v_C v_C^T as the “greatest lower bound” or lower envelope among rank-one matrices is inaccurate: the formal argument only establishes a maximal rank-one lower bound. Rank-one matrices aligned with other eigenvectors are generally incomparable with it in Löwner order.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a top-tier submission: no code is identified, and important details such as checkpoint identifiers, preprocessing, subset selection, random seeds, number of independent probe trials, numerical clipping, and complete timing procedures are missing.

strengths: The central random-projection estimator is simple, unbiased for a fixed dataset, and implementable with one additional backward pass per minibatch; the diagonal variance calculation provides a useful conditional coefficient-of-variation bound.
The paper develops a coherent connection between the categorical-simplex Fisher matrix and the network-parameter Fisher through the output Jacobian, with mostly self-contained derivations.
Experiments span NLP, vision, and audio architectures and compare against exact diagonal Fisher values on a fixed 8,192-example subset.
The presentation is generally organized and the limitations section acknowledges the absence of a downstream application.
weaknesses: The main methodological idea is essentially a standard random sketch of a matrix factor: if the Fisher is AA^T, then (Aξ)(Aξ)^T is unbiased. Calling this a novel family of “Hutchinson FIM” estimators overstates the conceptual novelty, and the paper does not adequately position the method against random-projection, stochastic curvature, and automatic-differentiation literature.

The comparison with Monte Carlo estimation is not controlled. The paper criticizes MC by randomizing input samples and invoking heavy-tailed input variance, while its own variance guarantee conditions on a fixed dataset. With minibatch sampling, the proposed estimator also inherits data-sampling variance. A one-backward-pass baseline that samples labels and uses independent random signs to cancel cross-example terms is also omitted.

The headline single-pass accuracy is misleading. Table 2 aggregates estimates across 128 batches with independent probes, so its roughly 0.1–0.2 relative errors benefit from about 128 backward passes and variance reduction across probes. The paper does not show the error distribution of an actual single-probe estimate, for which the stated CV bound of sqrt(2) is quite weak.

The evaluation is too limited to substantiate the broad claims: only diagonal entries are tested, although the work repeatedly claims estimation of the full metric tensor and its substructures. A single estimate of the full matrix is rank one, computationally prohibitive to materialize at modern parameter counts, and of questionable utility for natural-gradient or curvature applications without many probes.

The deterministic bounds are a major advertised contribution but receive essentially no empirical evaluation of tightness, usefulness, or computational tradeoffs on network Fisher matrices. The low-rank variants are evaluated only through diagonal RelMAE and can perform extremely poorly on several tasks.

Baselines and ablations are inadequate. There is no equal-compute label-MC comparison, no probe-count or batch-size study, no variance/error bars across random seeds, no comparison to efficient per-example-gradient or curvature-propagation implementations, and no downstream experiment demonstrating that the more accurate diagonal estimates improve optimization, pruning, or another application.

The chosen RelMAE is unstable for tiny Fisher entries and depends materially on the unexplained epsilon of 1e-12. Reporting a single parameter-wise mean hides the highly skewed distributions shown in the figures; medians, quantiles, normalized norm errors, and uncertainty across probes are needed. Interpreting RelMAE 0.2 as “±20% relative deviation” is also not statistically justified.

Claims of universality and production suitability are too strong. The construction explicitly sums over every output class, making it unattractive or infeasible for very large discrete output spaces and inapplicable as written to continuous outputs. Experiments stop at 100 classes and provide no memory analysis.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or artifact is identified, and important details about checkpoints, preprocessing, timing protocol, random seeds, and implementation of the exact reference and competing estimators are missing.

Several statements overstate what the theory establishes—for example, describing a CV bound of sqrt(2) as guaranteed estimation quality and suggesting moving averages across changing parameters recover the local Fisher rank without analyzing the bias caused by parameter drift. The manuscript also contains notation and proof-presentation issues that make some claims unnecessarily difficult to verify.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant contribution: an unbiased stochastic estimator of the Fisher information matrix that can be computed with one additional backward pass per minibatch.

Theoretical development is substantial. The paper derives deterministic upper and low-rank lower bounds from the categorical simplex, analyzes approximation errors, and proves unbiasedness and coordinate-wise variance bounds for the proposed estimators.

The empirical study covers six model–dataset settings spanning language, vision, and speech, with class counts from 2 to 100. The proposed estimator consistently achieves low relative error while retaining approximately empirical-Fisher runtime.

The exposition is generally coherent, with the relationship among core-space geometry, pullback Fisher matrices, deterministic approximations, and stochastic estimators developed systematically. Proofs are included in the appendix.
The paper appropriately acknowledges that it does not demonstrate benefits in a downstream application. I found no material unaddressed ethical concern.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is narrower than the paper's broad practical framing. It evaluates only diagonal-Fisher estimation and provides no optimizer, pruning, continual-learning, or other downstream experiment showing that the accuracy improvement matters in use.

The comparison protocol needs clarification. A conventional empirical diagonal FIM requires per-example gradients, yet it is described as a single-backward-pass baseline with nearly identical runtime. The exact batching, gradient aggregation, and implementation used for every estimator should be specified to ensure that all methods estimate the stated quantities.

Results appear to be based on a single stochastic realization and one fixed data subset. Error bars across probes or subsets, probe-count and batch-size ablations, and accuracy-versus-compute curves are missing. These are particularly important because the favorable approximately 0.2 RelMAE results aggregate independent probes over 128 minibatches.

The Monte Carlo estimator is excluded rather than compared under matched wall-clock or backward-pass budgets, and stronger computational baselines based on vectorized per-example gradients or modern autodifferentiation facilities are not considered.

The bounded coefficient of variation is established only for individual diagonal entries. A single full-matrix estimate is rank one, and the paper does not establish spectral- or Frobenius-norm accuracy, concentration of the diagonal vector, or the number of probes needed for reliable simultaneous estimation.

The random-projection construction is elegant but closely related to standard Hutchinson-style matrix sketching, so the novelty is moderate. Some broader statements—such as characterizing Adam as geometry-inspired and suggesting that the estimator is ready for evaluating the Hessian—are insufficiently precise or supported.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of code, seeds, precise checkpoints and fine-tuning details, estimator pseudocode, and memory measurements. These omissions make the reported exact-Fisher computation and speed comparisons difficult to independently verify.
